title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Vascular anomalies of the orbit represent a heterogeneous group of vascular lesions found within the orbit. A profound understanding of the natural course, appropriate nomenclature, clinical features, and imaging characteristics is essential for accurate diagnosis and appropriate management. This activity reviews the recently laid-out guidelines by the International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies (ISSVA) and describes the evaluation and management of OVAs. It also highlights the role of an interprofessional team-driven approach to deliver optimal outcomes.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Introduction
content: Orbital vascular anomalies (OVAs) comprise a diverse spectrum of lesions encountered within the orbit. Owing to the complex anatomy of the orbit, the controversial classification schemes for vascular anomalies, the variable clinical behavior of each subtype, and the limited understanding of the natural course of the disease, the management of OVAs is challenging. A meticulous evaluation of relevant imaging modalities and a coordinated, stepwise approach are crucial for establishing an accurate diagnosis and initiating an appropriate treatment strategy. [1]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Etiology

These lesions are composed of abnormal capillary, venous, lymphatic, arterial, or combined vascular elements and generally grow proportionally with the patient without spontaneous regression. Type 2: Low-flow (venous) lesions

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Etiology -- Subclassification of Vasoproliferative Tumors
content: Vasoproliferative tumors are classified according to biological behavior as benign, locally aggressive, or malignant. Benign vasoproliferative tumors include infantile hemangioma, the most common vascular tumor of infancy. Infantile hemangiomas may be superficial, deep, mixed (superficial and deep), or reticular or abortive forms characterized by minimal growth. Lesions may present with focal, multifocal, segmental, or indeterminate patterns that combine focal and segmental features. Infantile hemangiomas may also be associated with systemic syndromes, including PHACE syndrome (Posterior fossa malformations, Hemangioma, Arterial anomalies, Cardiovascular anomalies, Eye anomalies, and sternal clefting or supraumbilical raphe) and LUMBAR syndrome (Lower body hemangioma, Urogenital anomalies, Ulceration, Myelopathy, Bony deformities, Anorectal malformations, Arterial anomalies, and Renal anomalies). Congenital hemangiomas are fully developed at birth and are subclassified as rapidly involuting congenital hemangiomas (RICH), non-involuting congenital hemangiomas (NICH), or partially involuting congenital hemangiomas (PICH). Other benign vascular tumors include tufted angioma, epithelioid hemangioma, spindle cell hemangioma, pyogenic granuloma, and less common variants.

content: Subclassification of Vascular Malformations Vascular malformations are classified according to the type and combination of involved vascular channels. Simple vascular malformations involve a single vascular component and include capillary malformations, venous malformations (VM), lymphatic malformations, arteriovenous malformations (AVM), and arteriovenous fistulas (AVF). Lymphatic malformations may be macrocystic, microcystic, or mixed, while AVMs and AVFs are categorized as high-flow lesions.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Etiology -- Subclassification of Vasoproliferative Tumors
content: Combined vascular malformations consist of 2 or more vascular components within a single lesion. For example, lesions containing capillary, lymphatic, and arteriovenous components are termed capillary-lymphatic-arteriovenous malformations (CLAVM), while lesions composed of venous and lymphatic components are classified as venous-lymphatic malformations (VLM). Historically used terms such as “cavernous hemangioma” and “lymphangioma” should be avoided, as these lesions represent vascular malformations rather than true neoplasms. Lymphangiomas are more accurately classified as venous-lymphatic malformations, and cavernous hemangioma refers to a solitary, encapsulated venous malformation. Similarly, the terms “orbital varix” and “capillary hemangioma” should be avoided in contemporary clinical practice. [5]

content: Clinical staging of arteriovenous malformations was introduced by Schobinger in 1990 and remains widely used. Stage I represents the quiescent phase and is characterized by warm, pink-blue lesions. Stage II is marked by expansion with pulsation, thrill, and bruit. Stage III involves tissue destruction, including ulceration, bleeding, and dystrophic skin changes. Stage IV represents decompensation, with high-output cardiac failure. [7]

content: Anomalies of major named vessels, also referred to as channel-type or truncal vascular malformations, involve large-caliber lymphatic, arterial, or venous structures and present as fixed anatomic abnormalities. Syndromic vascular malformations include Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, Parks-Weber syndrome, Servelle-Martorell syndrome, and Sturge-Weber syndrome. These conditions are characterized by complex vascular anomalies, systemic or developmental abnormalities, and often require coordinated, multidisciplinary care.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Epidemiology
content: Orbital vascular anomalies (OVAs) account for approximately 10% of all orbital pathologies. [8] In a large study conducted in 2011, approximately one-fourth of cases of all orbital masses comprised “vasculogenic lesions,” whereas, in another series, the incidence was found to be 12%. [9] However, the studies did not use the most recent ISSVA guidelines for vascular anomalies and thus may have resulted in a gross underestimation. It is, therefore, hypothesized that OVAs might be the most common pathology found within the orbit. [10]

content: The rationale for the existing gender-specific differences among vascular anomalies remains unclear. Prematurity, low birth weight, and positive family history are the other predisposing factors of infantile hemangioma. [11]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Hemangioma
content: Hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumors of infancy and childhood, frequently affecting the head and neck region. They can be congenital or infantile (formerly termed juvenile hemangioma).

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Hemangioma
content: Infantile hemangioma, the most common type, clinically arises in the first 8 weeks and may be present at birth. Parents typically notice it later, when the baby is a few weeks old. A rapid proliferative phase ensues for 6 to 12 months, followed by an involuting, regressive phase lasting 5 to 9 years. During the proliferative phase, the tumor presents as a raised, rubbery, and red lesion, previously termed “strawberry hemangioma.” The involuted phase is characterized by scarring, wrinkling, and telangiectasia. [14] One must look for mechanical ptosis in cases of infantile hemangioma, which may result in refractive and stimulus-deprivation amblyopia. [15]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Hemangioma
content: Congenital hemangioma presents as full-blown lesions at birth with no proliferative phase. They are less likely to regress spontaneously. RICH, as the name suggests, undergoes a rapid phase of regression and disappears by 1 to 1.5 years of age. RICH may either present flat violaceous lesions or plaques with coarse telangiectasia or as raised greyish lesions, surrounded by a pale halo and multiple telangiectatic vessels. On the contrary, NICH doesn’t show regression and continues to increase in proportion to the child’s growth. [17]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Venous Malformations
content: Type 1: It is a low-flow, non-distensible OVM, wrongly termed a “cavernous hemangioma.” [18] According to the recently updated ISSVA nomenclature, it is better known as “cavernous venous malformation (CVM).” CVMs are prone to involve the middle third of the orbit and are primarily located in the intraconal space. [19] Almost two-thirds of patients are symptomatic, while the remaining third of cases are diagnosed coincidentally on imaging. Clinical features include gradual-onset axial proptosis, blurred vision, pain, or diplopia. The causes of visual impairment are hyperopic shift (correctable) and compressive optic neuropathy. Hyperopia in these patients is attributable to the lesion's flattening of the globe. It may also manifest as choroidal folds, disc changes ranging from swelling to optic atrophy, visual field defects, abnormal color vision, and afferent pupillary defects. Limitations of extraocular movements and ocular misalignment at primary gaze are observed in up to 30% of patients. [20] Gaze-evoked amaurosis (GEA) is one of the most unusual symptoms of orbital CVM, especially those occupying the extra- as well as the intra-conal spaces of the orbit. Axonal inhibition and optic nerve ischemia are the most likely causes of GEA. [21] [22] Optic nerve compromise and permanent axial length modification render the visual impairment irreversible. Recent reports have suggested a positive influence of hormones, such as estrogen or progesterone, on the clinical progression of CVMs. [23]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Venous Malformations
content: Type 2: Previously known as “orbital varices” - these are low-flow, distensible venous malformations that typically present during the second to third decade of life. Although they result from a congenital weakness in the wall of the veins leading to dilatation of the valveless veins of the orbit, they remain quiescent during childhood, which is then followed by growth around the pubertal period. The presenting clinical features include proptosis, diplopia, visual disturbances, or ecchymosis (due to hemorrhage or thrombosis). Almost 60% of distensible OVMs demonstrate distension on the dependent position or the Valsalva maneuver. The remaining 40% are usually the more posterior, deeper lesions and hence, show distensibility only on Valsalva-augmented imaging. Distensibility refers to an increase in proptosis due to increased intra-orbital venous pressure and the resultant expansion of the lesion. Hence, clinical evaluation of every suspected case is incomplete without examination at rest, in the dependent position, and during the Valsalva maneuver.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Lymphatic Malformations
content: Pure lymphatic malformations of the orbit are rare, as a variable venous component coexists in most cases. They consist of dilated lymphatic channels lined by podoplanin-positive endothelium. Lymphatic malformations are present since birth and can be radiologically classified as microcystic (<2 cm), macrocystic (>2 cm), or mixed, based on the size of the cavity within the lesion. Pure lymphatic malformations can present as an isolated, irregular mass in the anterior orbit. They don’t distend on a Valsalva maneuver and cannot be compressed. [24] Combined Venolymphatic Malformations

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Lymphatic Malformations
content: Microcystic lymphatic malformations typically infiltrate the tissue and present as diffuse thickening of the eyelid, conjunctiva, or anterior orbit. They can also affect the posterior orbit, sometimes extending till the apex, and manifest as gradual-onset proptosis. Bleeding into the lymphatic channels may lead to the formation of “chocolate cysts,” thereby exerting a mass effect. Sudden worsening of proptosis may result from bleeding within the lesion or from an upper respiratory infection of viral etiology that upregulates the lymphatic system and, in turn, causes rapid expansion of the lymphatic plexus. Massive hemorrhage may lead to motility limitation and visual impairment. Macrocystic lymphatic malformations are typically intraconal and, unlike microcystic lymphatic malformations, are less prone to intralesional hemorrhage. Ocular complications include corneal exposure, astigmatism, strabismus, optic neuropathy, and secondary glaucoma.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Arteriovenous Malformations
content: These lesions are characterized by rapid arterial flow into the draining venous channels, thereby bypassing the orbit's entire vascular system. Clinically, they present as pulsating proptosis. Thrombosis may manifest as an acute swelling, and hemorrhage may result in ecchymosis. AVMs may also elicit a bruit and cause pain and discomfort either at rest or when distended on the Valsalva maneuver or straining. Although rare, AVMs are invasive, depict an aggressive natural course, and tend to grow exponentially when treated inappropriately. Schobinger’s classification (as described above) not only provides insights into the clinical staging but also guides the management of these notorious lesions.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Arteriovenous Fistulas (AVFs)
content: Orbital AVFs, which are usually congenital arterio-venous connections fed by the branches of the ophthalmic artery with an absent intervening bed of capillaries, interspersed within a cellular stroma, clinically manifest as periocular swelling, dilated veins on the fundus, pulsations, and bruit, which typically reduce on compressing the ipsilateral common carotid artery (CCA), glaucoma, and visual deficits. In acquired AVFs, the anomalous connection is either due to trauma or idiopathic. The most common periocular AVF is the carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF). It can be of 2 types: direct and indirect.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Arteriovenous Fistulas (AVFs)
content: In direct CCF, trauma results in the formation of abnormal direct connections between the internal carotid artery (ICA) and the cavernous sinus. Other causes include Ehler-Danlos syndrome type IV, or iatrogenic procedures such as endarterectomy, trans-sphenoidal resection of the tumor in the pituitary region, percutaneous intervention in trigeminal neuralgia, and maxillofacial surgery. On the other hand, in indirect CCF (also known as a dural fistula), low-flow connections between the dural vein and internal or external carotid artery are formed due to an underlying systemic disease. The connections may involve the meningeal branch of the ICA, branches of the external carotid artery (ECA), or meningeal branches of both the ICA and the ECA.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- History and Physical -- Arteriovenous Fistulas (AVFs)
content: Among the branches of ECA, the internal maxillary artery is the most implicated vessel. The natural clinical course is usually indolent in cases of dural fistulas and acute in high-flow CCFs. The presenting features depend upon whether the fistula is high-flow or low-flow. The presence of pulsating proptosis and an objective bruit is a more specific feature of high-flow CCFs. Other clinical features include arterialization of vessels, increased episcleral venous pressure, neurogenic strabismus, most commonly 6th nerve palsy, owing to the central location of the 6th nerve adjacent to the ICA within the substance of the cavernous sinus, optic neuropathy, conjunctival chemosis, and congestion. [26]

content: Imaging forms a critical component of the diagnostic evaluation of OVAs and plays a crucial role in treatment planning. title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Evaluation -- Hemangioma
content: Evaluating whether the hemangioma is congenital or infantile is of paramount importance to determine the course of management. Investigations are needed to exclude the differential diagnosis of vascular rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) and other childhood malignancies. Arterial flow can be visualized on Color Doppler Ultrasonography (USG). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals a lesion that is slightly hypointense relative to the extraocular muscles on the T1-weighted (T1W) sequence, markedly enhances with contrast, and appears hyperintense on the T2-weighted (T2W) sequence. Involution-related and proliferative changes can be demonstrated on magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Evaluation -- Hemangioma
content: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) MRI has recently gained popularity due to its ability to qualitatively and quantitatively differentiate benign from malignant lesions using apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values. In infantile hemangioma, a bright ADC map reveals increased diffusion, whereas RMS shows restricted diffusion with lower diffusion coefficients. [27] On computed tomography, a hemangioma appears as a hyperdense lesion with homogeneous contrast enhancement. Expansion of the orbital cavity can be appreciated on imaging in case of large lesions, whereas small lesions produce scalloping of the bone adjacent to them. [28]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Evaluation -- Cavernous Venous Malformation (CVM)
content: USG (A- and B-scans) is a useful, noninvasive imaging modality, particularly for initial evaluation. A regular, round-shaped lesion with high internal reflectivity and moderate attenuation of echoes is characteristic of CVM. On computed tomography scan, CVM appears as a well-circumscribed, hyperdense, homogenous, intraconal lesion, seen as a discrete mass that does not directly adhere to the extra-ocular muscles and optic nerve and may occasionally erode the bone. Rarely can CVM encroach on the orbital apex, resembling the typical pear shape. Phleboliths, which are pathognomonic of venous malformations and are caused by chronic inflammation in long-standing cases, may appear as hyperdense, calcified areas within the mass. On Contrast-Enhancement, only minimal to mild contrast enhancement is seen in the early arterial phase, followed by diffuse enhancement during the late venous phase. This is because the blood flow within the lesion is independent of the orbital vasculature and is predominantly stagnant. Computed tomography angiography shows a nodular pattern of contrast enhancement in the early phase, attributable to small vessels within the lesion. However, radiation-associated ocular complications, mainly lens-related, limit its use as a routine procedure. CVM shows hypointense or isointense signals on T1-weighted (T1W) MRI sequences and heterogeneous hyperintensity on T2-weighted (T2W) MRI, due to intervening areas of thrombosis devoid of hyperintensity. [12]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Evaluation -- Cavernous Venous Malformation (CVM)
content: Dynamic investigations, such as Valsalva-augmented MRI, reveal no significant changes in the features. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is a non-invasive technique that provides direct static visualization of the orbital vasculature and indirectly yields limited information about blood flow characteristics. Dynamic assessment can be achieved using 3D time-of-flight and phase-contrast MRA. It is usually utilized to assess venous flow as a high-flow arterial component causes phase-related artifacts. Although 3D phase-contrast MRA better demonstrates flow characteristics, it is far more susceptible to motion artifacts than 2D MRA owing to its longer acquisition time.

content: CVMs appear relatively hyperintense on DWI, with ADC values ranging from 1.23 × 10 -3 mm 2 /s to 1.39 × 10 -3 mm 2 /s. This should be differentiated from lymphoma, which shows restricted diffusion and, hence, low signal intensity on ADC maps, with ADC values ranging from 0.44 x 10 mm/s to 0.92 x 10 mm/s. Orbital phlebography and arteriography have also been studied but are no longer used in current practice.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Evaluation -- A-V Malformations (AVMs)
content: On standard computed tomography and MRI scanning, AVMs are identified by the presence of cavernous sinus enlargement with lateral wall convexity, dilated superior ophthalmic vein, and an increase in extraocular muscle thickness. The presence of multiple flow voids, which correspond to high-flow vessels, is a characteristic feature on MRI. The TRICKS sequences help delineate the arterial and venous components as a function of time. AVMs appear irregularly tortuous and show vivid contrast enhancement with or without intracranial involvement. Aneurysms are usually located at the origin of the ophthalmic artery and, rarely, within the orbit, and can be detected on imaging.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Evaluation -- A-V Malformations (AVMs)
content: Digital subtraction angiography, in which contrast is directly injected into the feeding vessels and then digitally acquired, is the gold standard for evaluating AVMs. It effectively maps the entire vasculature by delineating the draining venous component and arterial feeder vessels. DSA is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Non-invasive neuroimaging modalities, including computed tomography angiography and magnetic resonance angiography, are highly sensitive for CCFs. High-flow fistulas demonstrate rapid sinus filling with minimal to absent filling of intracranial vessels. In contrast, low-flow dural fistulas show delayed, slow filling with the intact filling of the intracranial vasculature. Demonstration of nidus on angiography almost always ascertains the diagnosis of an arterio-venous malformation and is typically absent in cases of arteriovenous fistula. [33]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Treatment / Management -- Hemangioma
content: As discussed above, recognizing infantile hemangioma and distinguishing it from congenital hemangioma is vital, as the preferred treatment differs. Medical management, primarily beta-blockers, namely oral propranolol and topical timolol maleate, forms the mainstay of treatment of hemangioma. The child must undergo a comprehensive cardiac evaluation before initiation of therapy. According to the infantile hemangioma guidelines, a trial of atenolol therapy may be considered in patients for whom propranolol is contraindicated or not tolerated. A gel-forming solution of timolol is as effective as systemic therapy and is associated with negligible life-threatening complications.

content: Before the advent of beta-blocker use, systemic and intralesional steroid therapy was the first line of management. The role of intralesional bevacizumab is unclear, and the drug is under experimental phases. Lasers are not recommended for infantile hemangioma, except for the treatment of residual skin changes and scars following resolution. [34]

content: The therapy goals in venous malformations are to reduce the symptoms (persistent pain), improve function (optic neuropathy and corneal exposure leading to visual loss, tense hemorrhage), and achieve acceptable cosmesis. Management options for orbital venous malformations are as follows: [6] Observation: for asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic cases Surgery: for isolated, localized lesions where complete excision is feasible with minimal morbidity. content: Intra-operative mapping and glue (n-butyl cyanoacrylate) embolization aid in surgical excision, thereby reducing the risk of rupture and troublesome bleeding. Macrocystic lymphatic malformations respond well to sclerotherapy, whereas microcystic lymphatic malformations, in addition to sclerotherapy, may require surgical intervention. title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Treatment / Management -- A-V Malformations (AVMs)
content: A crisp understanding of the hemodynamics of AVMs facilitates decision-making regarding the appropriate management strategy. A combined approach of preoperative embolization followed by resection of the nidus is the preferred management strategy. Caution should be maintained to completely resect the nidus to prevent recurrence, as a recurrent AVM grows exponentially and is more cumbersome to treat. Not all AVMs are amenable to resection. Some of these can be managed conservatively as they may carry significant surgical morbidity and iatrogenic risk of damaging surrounding structures. Specific indications of surgical excision include recurrent hemorrhage, pain, and associated visual disturbances.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Treatment / Management -- A-V Malformations (AVMs)
content: Successful closure of high-flow direct CCFs can be achieved with minimal morbidity using recently emerged endovascular techniques. Endovascular embolization via the transarterial route into the cavernous sinus, using materials such as detachable balloon, n-butyl cyanoacrylate, or ethyl vinyl alcohol polymer, is the preferred management strategy. Recently, due to the non-availability of detachable balloons, coiling has emerged as the treatment modality of choice. [42] [43] [44] In cases with an associated ICA wall tear, flow-diverting stent-assisted embolization is a viable option because it avoids misdirection of material into the arterial circulation, thereby preventing life-threatening complications. [45] Endovascular intervention in high-flow CCFs has shown 90-100% success rates with low (<1%) mortality. [46] [47] [48]

content: While performing a carotid massage, it is advisable to use the contralateral hand to compress the ipsilateral ICA. This is because, if cerebral ischemia results from reduced arterial pressure, contralateral hemiparesis itself reduces the pressure on the artery, thereby creating a feedback loop. Carotid compression in the presence of atherosclerotic disease further aggravates the risk of stroke due to pre-existing carotid insufficiency. The additional technique involves superomedial SOV compression in these cases. [26]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of orbital vascular anomalies depends upon whether the mass is intraconal or extraconal, the nature of the lesion, and its relative localization within the orbit. The differential diagnoses for a well-circumscribed solid tumor include cavernous venous malformation, schwannoma, solitary fibrous tumor, lymphoid lesions of the orbit (lymphoma), benign reactive hyperplasia, orbital metastasis, fibrous histiocytoma, or neurofibroma.

content: Every orbital vascular anomaly behaves distinctly. The prognosis depends primarily on the nature, extent, and localization of the lesion, visual acuity, and the status of the optic nerve.

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Complications
content: Lesions extending to the orbital apex, large-sized anomalies, and those associated with optic neuropathy are associated with a higher risk of vision-related complications following surgery. Other possible complications include ptosis and motility limitations, which usually resolve within a few months. Recurrence is not uncommon. The risk of amblyopia should be a key consideration when managing childhood vascular anomalies. [52]

title: Orbital Vascular Anomalies -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Management of orbital vascular anomalies is complex and challenging. A team-driven approach is recommended to avoid misdiagnosis and mismanagement of OVAs. Interprofessional collaboration among ophthalmologists specializing in orbit, an interventional neuroradiologist, and a pediatrician is essential. Shared decision-making, coordination, and effective communication are critical to maximizing favorable outcomes.
